Abstract
With the rapid advancement of information technology and artificial intelli-
gence, the energy efficiency bottleneck of the von Neumann architecture and
the scaling limits of silicon‐based semiconductors are increasingly constrain-
ing improvements in computing performance. Neuromorphic computing, by
emulating the cooperative behavior of neurons and synapses in the brain,
enables the integration of computation and memory, offering a promising
route toward next‐generation low‐power and high‐performance computing. As
a key strategy for artificial synapse implementation, optoelectronic synapses
exhibit ultrafast response, broad bandwidth, and contactless optical signal
transmission, conferring significant advantages in information sensing,
transmission, and storage. In particular, two‐dimensional (2D) transition
metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with their atomic‐scale thickness, tunable
bandgaps, and outstanding optoelectronic properties provide an ideal material
platform for highly integrated optoelectronic synaptic devices. This review
presents a comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts of artificial
synapses and synaptic plasticity, examines the device architectures and
operating mechanisms of optoelectronic synapses based on 2D TMDs along
with their applications in neuromorphic visual systems and neuromorphic
computing, and further discusses the key challenges and future research di-
rections in this area.

INTRODUCTION
Given the rapid breakthroughs in information technology
and artificial intelligence, the amount of information
generated in modern society is growing exponentially.
However, the traditional von Neumann computing ar-
chitecture, due to the separation of processing and
memory units, struggles to achieve an effective balance
between power consumption and computational effi-
ciency, and is increasingly facing performance bottle-
necks.1–10 At the same time, as transistor dimensions
continue to reduce, silicon‐based semiconductors suffer
from severe performance degradation, and the scaling of
integrated circuits is approaching physical limits.11 As a
result, Moore's law is becoming difficult to sustain,
posing
significant
constraints
on
the
continuous
improvement of computing performance.12
In contrast, the human brain performs highly efficient
parallel computation with minimal power consumption,
enabled by the cooperative interaction of neurons and
synapses.13–20 Inspired by this, Carver Mead introduced
the concept of neuromorphic computing, with the central
aim of emulating the brain's integrated mechanisms of
computation and memory.21 As the fundamental building
blocks of neural networks, synapses transmit information
by modulating the connection strengths between neurons
and play a crucial role in neural signal processing.22 With
the continuous development of neuromorphic computing,
researchers have devoted considerable effort to the design
and fabrication of artificial synapses capable of emulating
the functions of biological synapses.23–30
Optoelectronic synaptic devices, as a new generation
of artificial synapses, regulate conductance through op-
tical signals to achieve information sensing, transmission,
and storage.31–35 Compared with conventional electronic
synaptic devices, they demonstrate significant advantages
in response speed, bandwidth, and energy efficiency. The
contactless transmission of optical signals not only en-
dows these devices with enhanced parallel processing
capabilities but also effectively reduces the complexity of
circuit interconnections, providing a feasible pathway for
large‐scale neuromorphic computing.36 Moreover, opto-
electronic synaptic devices can emulate biological visual
systems, showing broad application prospects in tasks
such as image perception, processing, motion detection,
and visual adaptation.37–41

morphic computing hardware.42,43 Among various 2D
materials, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are
widely regarded as ideal candidates for optoelectronic
devices owing to their tunable bandgaps, exceptional
optical and electrical properties, and potential for large‐

Furthermore, through strategies such as heterostructure

computing hardware.49–52
In conclusion, the integration of optoelectronic syn-
apses with 2D TMDs offers an efficient, scalable, and low‐
power technological pathway for neuromorphic vision
systems and neuromorphic computing. In recent years,
2D‐TMD‐based optoelectronic synapses have made sig-
nificant progress in synaptic plasticity emulation, neuro-
morphic vision systems, and neuromorphic computing,
laying a solid foundation for the development of next‐
generation neuromorphic hardware.53–60 This review sys-

ARTIFICIAL SYNAPSES AND
SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
The human brain is a highly parallel computing system
responsible for processing various types of information,
including learning, memory, perception, language, motor
control, and expression. It consists of approximately 1011
neurons and 1015 synapses, forming a highly inter-
connected and structurally complex neural network with
powerful large‐scale parallel computing capabilities.70,71
A synapse is defined as the junction between two neu-
rons, serving as the critical pathway for the transmission
of neural signals from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic
neuron.72,73
Artificial
synapses
in
neuromorphic
computing systems are designed to emulate the function
of biological synapses. As shown in Figure 2A, a typical
device comprises a top electrode representing the pre-
synaptic neuron, a bottom electrode corresponding to the
postsynaptic neuron, and an intermediate memristive
layer that reproduces synaptic behavior.74
The synaptic weight defines the strength of the
connection between two neurons. In artificial synapses, it

By contrast, LTP is widely recognized as the biological

The main forms of STP include short‐term potentia-
tion (STP1), short‐term depression (STD), paired‐pulse
facilitation (PPF), and paired‐pulse depression (PPD).
STP1 refers to a transient increase in synaptic weight
following stimulation, which rapidly returns to its base-
line state. In contrast, STD describes a temporary
reduction in synaptic weight after stimulation followed
by a quick recovery to the initial level. PPF and PPD refer
to successive short‐term enhancement and suppression of
synaptic strength, respectively, induced by the interaction
of closely spaced input pulses. Specifically, when two
stimuli are applied to a neuron in rapid succession, the
response to the second stimulus (A2) can be either
stronger or weaker than the first stimulus (A1), resulting
in PPF or PPD, respectively. This response can be quan-
tified by the PPF or PPD index, defined as the amplitude
ratio A2/A1, as illustrated in Figure 2B.83 The PPF/PPD
index can be fitted using a double‐exponential function:78

widely regarded as key molecular mechanisms underlying

synaptic weight depend on the relative timing between
presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes (tpost −tpre).88 As early
as 1949, D. Hebb observed the influence of postsynaptic
activity on the presynaptic neuron.89 According to the
classical Hebbian learning rule, when a presynaptic spike
precedes a postsynaptic spike (tpost −tpre > 0), the synaptic
weight is increased, resulting in LTP1; conversely, if
the postsynaptic spike precedes the presynaptic one
(tpost −tpre < 0), LTD typically occurs.90 STDP is essentially
an extension of the Hebbian learning rule. Based on the
relationship between synaptic weight changes and the
timing of spikes, STDP can be further categorized into four
types: asymmetric Hebbian, symmetric Hebbian, asym-
metric
anti‐Hebbian,
and
symmetric
anti‐Hebbian
learning rules (Figure 2C).91 In addition to STDP, SRDP
is regarded as another fundamental learning mechanism
for LTP. In SRDP, synaptic weight changes depend on the
frequency of presynaptic spikes: a series of high‐frequency
presynaptic spikes (20–100 Hz) typically induces LTP1,
whereas low‐frequency stimulation (1–5 Hz) generally
leads to LTD.92,93

Two‐terminal optoelectronic
synaptic devices
Two‐terminal
synaptic
devices
achieve
synaptic
re-
sponses by modulating the conductivity of the material
between two electrodes. One electrode acts as the pre-
synaptic neuron applying voltage pulses, while the other
serves as the postsynaptic neuron generating postsynaptic
currents.94 In two‐terminal optoelectronic synaptic de-
vices, the core component is a photosensitive material
with intrinsic memory effects, in which the resistance
state strongly depends on its history, thereby enabling the
emulation of synaptic connections between neurons.
Owing to their outstanding optical and electrical prop-
erties, 2D TMDs have emerged as promising candidates
for constructing optoelectronic synapses.45,46
3.1.1
|
Two‐terminal optoelectronic synaptic
devices based on a single material
Two‐terminal optoelectronic synaptic devices composed of
a single material offer advantages such as a simple struc-
ture and low power consumption, enabling them to meet
the high connectivity and processor density requirements
for emulating efficient biological systems.95 Such devices
typically rely on intrinsic defects within the material to
capture and gradually release photogenerated carriers.
These devices can be categorized according to defect type:
one group utilizes intrinsic defects in 2D TMDs for carrier
trapping, while the other enhances carrier trapping or
suppresses carrier recombination through band‐structure
engineering by intentionally introducing defects, thereby
improving optoelectronic synaptic performance.52,63,68,96

Sulfur and selenium vacancies are the most prevalent
intrinsic defects in 2D TMDs such as MoS2, ReS2, MoSe2,
and WSe2. These vacancies introduce localized energy
states within the bandgap, which can trap photogenerated
carriers and gradually release them over time, thereby
enabling persistent conductance modulation and the
realization of optoelectronic synaptic functionalities. Chen
et al. developed an optoelectronic synaptic device based on
ReS2 (Figure 3A). The core operation mechanism of this
device is the persistent photoconductivity (PPC) effect,
originating from deep and shallow trap levels induced by
sulfur vacancies in ReS2. Under photoexcitation, electrons
in the conduction band can recombine directly with holes
in the valence band (①). However, some electrons are
captured by trap states (②: deep traps; ③: shallow traps) and
require thermal activation to be released back into the
conduction band before recombination. Similarly, trapped
holes (④: deep traps; ⑤: shallow traps) must be thermally
excited back into the valence band to recombine with
electrons. Consequently, the recombination dynamics of
photogenerated carriers are jointly governed by the fast
direct recombination process and the slower trap‐release
process, thereby prolonging the carrier lifetime, as illus-
trated in Figure 3B.63 Similarly, selenium vacancies in
MoSe2 also contribute to its optoelectronic synaptic per-
formance, enabling the emulation of fundamental biolog-
ical synaptic behaviors such as PPF, as shown in
Figure 3C,D.96

plished through various methods, including surface
plasma treatment, irradiation, and doping.52,98,99 Among

enabling the development of high‐performance opto-

induced lattice distortion facilitated the formation of Se
vacancies. These defect states can act as charge traps,
significantly prolonging the decay time of the photo-
response and thereby imparting memory functionality to
the device. Compared to pristine MoSe2, which exhibits a
rapid photoresponse, Te‐doped devices display signifi-

Two‐terminal optoelectronic synaptic
devices based on heterostructures
Van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures are constructed by
stacking 2D materials with other one‐, two‐, or three‐
dimensional materials, where the layers are bound
together by weak vdW interactions. Such structures
feature
atomically
sharp
interfaces,
minimal
lattice
mismatch, and tunable optical and electronic properties.
Exploiting heterostructures is a common strategy to
realize or enhance optoelectronic synaptic performance.
Although more difficult to fabricate than single‐material
devices, vdW heterostructures often exhibit emergent
properties and functionalities that exceed those of their
individual constituents.58,61 In optoelectronic synaptic
devices, heterostructures can impart or optimize synaptic
functions through multiple mechanisms. On one hand,
charge transfer and trapping between different materials
can enable optoelectronic synaptic behavior.100 On the
other hand, band alignment engineering can facilitate the
separation of photogenerated carriers, thereby improving
photoelectric
conversion
efficiency.101
Moreover,
by
leveraging the complementary advantages of different
materials, heterostructures can be designed to achieve
multifunctionality and broad‐wavelength photoresponse,
further expanding their potential application.64
By combining 2D TMDs with another defect‐rich
material to form a heterostructure, defects in the adja-
cent material can efficiently capture and confine photo-
generated carriers in the TMDs, thereby endowing the
device with excellent optoelectronic synaptic perfor-
mance. This strategy not only preserves the high crys-
tallinity of the original TMDs but also introduces
abundant defect centers for charge storage, providing
new avenues for the design and optimization of high‐
performance, low‐power optoelectronic synaptic devices.
For example, Deng et al. fabricated Fe7S8/MoS2 hetero-
structures, where Fe7S8, rich in intrinsic defects, effec-
tively
captures
photogenerated
carriers
in
MoS2,
endowing the device with excellent charge‐trapping and
storage capabilities and enabling integrated sensing and
memory functions (Figure 4A,B). With increasing optical
stimulation, the device exhibits a transition from STP1 to
LTP1, as shown in Figure 4C.100
By rationally designing the band structure of the
heterostructure, photogenerated carriers can be effi-
ciently separated, and internal or interfacial defects can
capture these carriers, thereby suppressing electron‐hole
recombination and further enhancing optoelectronic
synaptic performance. For instance, in SnSe/MoS2 p‐n
junctions (Figure 4D), the equilibrium band structure
forms a type‐II band alignment, where the conduction
band minimum and valence band maximum lie in
different materials, resulting in staggered bands. This
configuration enables spatial separation of electrons and
holes across the interface, which is advantageous for
charge separation in optoelectronic devices. After mild
UV‐ozone treatment, a thin oxide layer forms on the
device surface. Under light illumination, electrons from
the valence bands of SnSe and MoS2 are excited into the
conduction band of MoS2 and into trap states within the
oxide layer, reducing the Schottky barrier at the MoS2/
electrode interface and generating an enhanced photo-
current. Driven by the built‐in electric field at the SnSe/
MoS2 interface, holes in the MoS2 valence band migrate
toward the SnSe layer, while electrons remain confined
within MoS2 as illustrated in Figure 4E. This spatial
separation effectively delays electron‐hole recombination,
resulting in pronounced optoelectronic synaptic plasticity
(Figure 4F).101

Three‐terminal optoelectronic
synaptic devices
Two‐terminal synaptic devices, owing to their structural
simplicity, are well suited for high‐density integration.
However, their ability to emulate complex biological
synaptic functions is limited, as signal transmission and
weight modulation share the same physical pathway,
hindering simultaneous real‐time monitoring and adap-
tive learning. Three‐terminal synaptic devices based on
field‐effect transistors (FETs) overcome this limitation by
introducing an independent control terminal that de-
couples these functions.95 Depending on their operation
mechanism, such FETs include optoelectronic FETs
(OpFETs), floating‐gate FETs (FGFETs), and ferroelectric
FETs (FeFETs).
2D TMDs exhibit gate‐tunable conductivity and strong
photoresponsivity, allowing them to serve simultaneously
as both the channel and photosensitive layers in FETs—
making them ideal for constructing three‐terminal opto-
electronic synaptic devices. Few‐layer hexagonal boron
nitride (h‐BN) with a wide optical bandgap (~6 eV) func-
tions as an excellent electrical insulator and a critical
tunneling barrier in FGFETs.66 In addition to h‐BN,
several other materials have been investigated as tunneling
layers in FGFETs. Notably, LaOCl (bandgap ≈5.54 eV,
dielectric constant ≈13.8) and β‐Ga2O3 (bandgap ≈4.9 eV,
dielectric constant ≈10) have demonstrated considerable
potential for enhancing device performance.102,103 Certain

Optoelectronic synaptic devices based
on FGFETs
FGFETs are a class of transistors based on 2D vdW het-
erostructures, typically consisting of a floating‐gate layer
(e.g., graphene), a tunneling layer (e.g., h‐BN), and a
channel layer (e.g., ReS2).66 Their core operation princi-
ple relies on charge tunneling to achieve nonvolatile
memory functionality. When integrated with photosen-
sitive materials, FGFET‐based optoelectronic synaptic
devices
can
emulate
biological
synaptic
behaviors,
exhibiting plasticity modulated by optical stimuli.
Yang et al. demonstrated a FGFET based on a ReS2/h‐
BN/graphene vdW heterostructure, in which ReS2 serves as
the channel layer, h‐BN as the tunneling barrier, and gra-
phene as the floating gate, as shown in Figure 6A. Under
optical illumination, abundant electron‐hole pairs are
generated in the ReS2 channel. Driven by the charge storage
capability of graphene, the photogenerated holes tunnel
through the h‐BN barrier and become trapped in the gra-
phene floating gate. The mechanism of optical erasing is
illustrated by the energy band diagram in Figure 6B. Owing
tothecapacitivecouplingofgrapheneandtheaccumulation
of photogenerated carriers, the ReS2 channel conductance
exhibits nonvolatile enhancement, corresponding to opto-
electronic synaptic plasticity and enabling the emulation of
essential biological functions such as PPF, as shown in
Figure 6C. Notably, this device achieves ultrahigh‐precision
multibit optical synaptic weight modulation with up to 1024
discrete states (10‐bit resolution), representing the highest
performance reported to date for 2D‐material‐based opto-
electronic FGFETs.66

Li et al. reported an optoelectronic synaptic device
based on an In2Se3/WSe2 ferroelectric heterostructure,

reversible polarization switching under external electric

channel layer responsible for photocarrier generation and
transport (Figure 6D). This heterostructure integrates the
nonvolatile memory characteristics of ferroelectrics with
the high photoresponsivity of the semiconductor channel.
As illustrated in Figure 6E,F, the operation mechanism
relies on the interplay between ferroelectric polarization
modulation and the built‐in electric field. The type‐II
band alignment between α‐In2Se3 and WSe2 facilitates
efficient electron transport across the interface and es-
tablishes a built‐in electric field (Ebi) directed from α‐
In2Se3 to WSe2. In addition, the ferroelectric polarization
of α‐In2Se3 induces a depolarization field (Edep). Under
upward polarization (Pup), screening charges of opposite
polarity accumulate near the α‐In2Se3 surface, generating
a screening field (Esc) that counteracts Edep. Upon illu-
mination, photogenerated electron‐hole pairs are sepa-

α‐In2Se3,
neutralizing the interfacial screening charges and thereby
significantly weakening Esc. Consequently, the depolari-
zation field Edep gradually drives the polarization to
switch from Pup to downward polarization (Pdown). After
the light is removed, Ebi helps maintain part of the po-
larization in the Pdown state, allowing this polarization
state to persist in the dark and leading to controllable
excitatory postsynaptic currents. Importantly, the In2Se3/

NEUROMORPHIC APPLICATIONS
Traditional optoelectronic information systems based on
the von Neumann architecture suffer from severe bot-
tlenecks in computational efficiency and energy con-
sumption due to the physical separation of memory and
processing units.6 With the explosive growth of data in
the information era, there is an urgent demand for inte-
grated device architectures capable of simultaneously
performing optical sensing, information storage, and data
processing in order to enhance computational efficiency
and significantly reduce power consumption. Inspired by
the human visual system, optoelectronic synaptic devices
realize perception‐memory‐processing integration within
a single device, thereby demonstrating broad application
prospects in artificial visual systems and neuromorphic
computing. In recent years, 2D‐TMD‐based optoelec-
tronic synaptic devices have shown tremendous potential
in applications such as image perception, image denois-
ing, motion detection, visual adaptation, and neuro-
morphic
computing.37–41,112–114

tion but also carries out preliminary preprocessing at the
retinal level to improve data quality and reduce the
computational load for subsequent processing.100 The
visual cortex then processes this simplified information
for more complex analysis. Similarly, optoelectronic
synaptic devices can achieve integrated perception and
processing. For instance, an oxygen‐doped MoS2 opto-
electronic synapse has been demonstrated for denoising
the preprocessing of license plate images. Figure 7D il-
lustrates the noise reduction process of the device. The
device effectively recovers key image features and sup-
presses background noise, offering a promising route
toward energy‐efficient neuromorphic visual systems.38
Optoelectronic synaptic devices can also be extended
to motion target detection. As shown in Figure 7E, MoS2‐
based optoelectronic synapses can recognize the motion
of individuals riding electric bicycles under visible light
or broadband illumination in bright environments. More
importantly, in dark conditions, they can still achieve
motion detection with the assistance of near‐infrared
radiation from the broadband spectrum, enabling all‐
day motion recognition capability.40
In addition, a bio‐inspired artificial neuron module
based on monolayer MoS2 integrates the functions of dy-
namic random‐access memory (DRAM) and an inverter,
thereby emulating the intrinsic synaptic plasticity of
biological neurons and exhibiting visual adaptation
(Figure 7F). By tuning the gate voltage (VS) of the DRAM
device, the photosensitivity can be flexibly modulated to
mimic the light adaptation of cone cells and the dark
adaptation of rod cells in the human eye. Specifically,
lowering VS corresponds tocone‐cell‐like adaptation under
strong illumination, while increasing VS and enhancing
the leakage current correspond to rod‐cell‐like adaptation
under weak illumination. Consequently, under appro-
priate VS conditions, both overly bright and overly dark
images can be effectively recognized, providing a robust
hardware foundation for constructing highly adaptive
neuromorphic visual systems.41

and modulated via artificial synapses—mimicking the

physical device designs.115,116

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of information technology and artificial intelli- gence, the energy efficiency bottleneck of the von Neumann architecture and the scaling limits of silicon‐based semiconductors are increasingly constrain- ing improvements in computing performance. Neuromorphic computing, by emulating the cooperative behavior of neurons and synapses in the brain, enables the integration of computation and memory, offering a promising route toward next‐generation low‐power and high‐performance computing. As a key strategy for artificial synapse implementation, optoelectronic synapses exhibit ultrafast response, broad bandwidth, and contactless optical signal transmission, conferring significant advantages in information sensing, transmission, and storage. In particular, two‐dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with their atomic‐scale thickness, tunable bandgaps, and outstanding optoelectronic properties provide an ideal material platform for highly integrated optoelectronic synaptic devices. This review presents a comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts of artificial synapses and synaptic plasticity, examines the device architectures and operating mechanisms of optoelectronic synapses based on 2D TMDs along with their applications in neuromorphic visual systems and neuromorphic computing, and further discusses the key challenges and future research di- rections in this area.
